ap_psychology-m01.stem: Researchers want to track, within milliseconds, how the brain's electrical activity changes while a person hears a spoken word. Which technique is best suited, and why?

options.text: fMRI, because it measures the timing of neural firing more precisely than any other imaging technique does.
options.why: fMRI follows blood flow, which changes over seconds, so its timing is much coarser than EEG's.

options.text: A CT scan, because it shows the brain's activity in real time as the person listens to the word.
options.why: A CT scan shows brain structure and does not record activity as it changes over time.

options.text: EEG, because it records the brain's electrical activity with very fine timing.
options.why: EEG detects electrical activity at the scalp with a time resolution of milliseconds, which fits a question about rapid timing.

options.text: A lesion study, because damage to one area shows exactly when that area becomes active during listening.
options.why: A lesion study shows what an area is needed for, not the moment-to-moment timing of activity.

options.why: Melatonin regulates sleep and oxytocin is linked to bonding, not to hunger and fullness.

options.text: Ghrelin rose when she skipped lunch, and leptin signaled fullness after dinner.
options.why: Ghrelin increases hunger when the stomach is empty, and leptin, released from fat cells, signals that the body has enough energy.

options.text: Leptin rose when she skipped lunch, and ghrelin signaled fullness after dinner.
options.why: The roles are reversed: ghrelin promotes hunger and leptin signals fullness.

options.text: Chunking groups items into meaningful units, so working memory holds more information.
options.why: Short-term memory is limited, and organizing items into larger meaningful units lets it hold more of the information.

options.text: Implicit memory stores the order outside of awareness, so the waiter does not need to use any mental strategy.
options.why: Remembering an order by regrouping is a conscious, explicit strategy and not implicit memory.

options.text: Sensory memory holds eight items for several minutes, so the waiter did not need any strategy to remember the order.
options.why: Sensory memory holds information only for a very brief time, so a strategy is needed to retain items.

options.text: Maintenance rehearsal transfers every item automatically to long-term memory by repeating each item several times.
options.why: Repeating items does not guarantee transfer to long-term memory, and the waiter is regrouping items, not repeating them.

options.text: Long-term memory held all of the letters, but retrieval cues were missing when she tried to report the display.
options.why: The display lasted a fraction of a second, so the letters were not stored in long-term memory.

options.text: Implicit memory held the letters outside of awareness, so she could not report any of them in words.
options.why: She could report four letters, so the explanation does not involve unreportable implicit memory.

options.text: Short-term memory held all 12 letters, but the letters decayed during the seconds she took to start reporting them.
options.why: Short-term memory capacity is limited to far fewer items than 12.

When one confederate chooses the correct line, the participant's agreement with the wrong majority drops sharply. Which statement best explains the change?

options.text: Conformity decreases when a group member breaks unanimity, because the participant is no longer alone in disagreeing.
options.why: A single dissenter weakens the group's unanimity and gives the participant social support for disagreeing with the majority.

options.text: Conformity is unaffected by whether the group is unanimous, because the participant's judgments depend only on the lines.
options.why: Unanimity affects conformity; the sharp drop shows that the group's makeup mattered.

options.text: Conformity increases when a group member breaks unanimity, because the participant must now choose between two groups.
options.why: A dissenter reduces rather than increases conformity pressure.

options.text: Conformity decreases because the dissenter's behavior makes the participant unable to see the lines clearly.
options.why: The dissenter does not change what the participant can see; the change reflects social pressure.

Residents who signed volunteer far more often than residents who were asked to volunteer without being asked to sign. Which concept best explains this?

options.text: The foot-in-the-door phenomenon: agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a larger one.
options.why: Compliance with a small request can change how people see themselves and raise the likelihood of agreeing to a larger request.

options.text: Group polarization explains it, because the signatures of other residents made the petition's supporters more extreme.

options.why: Social facilitation concerns performance in the presence of others and does not describe agreement to later requests.

ap_psychology-m08.stem: A study with 80 American college students finds that people explain others' failures mostly by their personalities. The authors conclude that this is a universal human tendency. Which response is the most appropriate?

options.text: The conclusion is justified, because college students are the only group whose attributions can be studied scientifically.
options.why: Other groups can be studied, so this reason does not justify a universal claim.

options.text: The conclusion is justified, because a sample of 80 participants is always large enough to describe all human beings.
options.why: Sample size does not make a narrow sample representative of all people.

options.text: The conclusion is unjustified, because explaining others' failures by personality is impossible to measure in any sample.
options.why: Attributional styles can be measured; the problem is generalization, not measurement.

options.text: The sample is limited to one culture and one student group, so the claim should be tested in other cultures first.
